report.tagline: Apple's built-in wallet on iPhone and Apple Watch that lets you tap to pay in shops, pay in one tap online, and carry cards, tickets, keys and IDs.
report.simpleSummary: Apple Pay lets you pay by holding your iPhone or Apple Watch near a card machine. You add your bank card to the Wallet app once, then double-click the side button, look at the phone and tap. The shop never sees your real card number. Shoppers and shops pay Apple nothing; instead the bank that issued your card pays Apple a small cut of each payment.

overview.whatItDoes: Apple Pay turns iPhones and Apple Watches into payment cards that work in shops, in apps and online. Apple Wallet holds bank cards plus Apple Card, Apple Cash, transit cards, boarding passes, event tickets, car and hotel keys, and in some US states driving licences. Merchants can also take card payments on their own iPhone with Tap to Pay on iPhone. For years Apple was the only one allowed to use the iPhone's tap-to-pay chip, which is why regulators are now forcing it open.
howItWorks: You add a card in Wallet. Your bank and Visa or Mastercard create a token, a stand-in card number, which is stored in a secure chip in the phone called the Secure Element.
At a shop, you double-click the side button, look at the phone for Face ID, then hold it near the terminal. The phone sends the token over NFC.
The bank approves the payment as normal. The shop sees only the token, not your real card number, so a data leak at the shop does not expose your card.
Apple charges the card-issuing bank a small fee on each payment. Banks agreed to this in return for being in Apple Pay.
Online and in apps, an Apple Pay button fills in card, address and email in one tap with Face ID.
Express Transit lets you tap through London Underground gates without unlocking the phone.
overview.valueProposition: The fastest and safest way to pay with an iPhone: no card to carry, no card number shared with shops, and checkout online in one tap.

businessModel.summary: Apple Pay is free for shoppers and merchants. Apple earns a small fee from banks on each payment and fees from some third-party NFC apps. The bigger value is that it keeps people buying iPhones and Apple Watches.

revenueStreams.detail: Banks pay Apple a share of each Apple Pay transaction, reported at about 0.15% of US credit spend.
Revenue share from Apple's card partner bank in the US.
Fees from third-party payment apps that use iPhone NFC outside the EU.
Indirect: a daily payment habit makes users less likely to switch to Android.

businessModel.pricing: Free for shoppers and merchants. Banks pay Apple fees that are not public. Merchants pay their normal card processing fees.
costDrivers: Engineering for security, the Secure Element and Wallet
Bank and card network partnerships in each country
Legal and regulatory costs in the EU, UK and US
businessModel.unitEconomics: Take a £4 coffee paid with Apple Pay on a credit card. If Apple's fee is about 0.15%, Apple earns 0.6p. A user who spends £10,000 a year through Apple Pay on credit earns Apple about £15. Small per person, but across hundreds of millions of users it is likely billions of dollars a year (estimate). Apple's cost per payment is close to zero, since the bank and network do the work. The real value is that each tap makes the £1,000 iPhone harder to leave.

howTheyGetUsers: Pre-installed on every iPhone and Apple Watch, with prompts during setup
Banks push customers to add cards from their own apps
Transit systems like TfL accepting phone taps
Merchants adding Apple Pay buttons to raise conversion
whatBringsUsersBack: Passes, keys and tickets stored in Wallet
growth.moat: Apple controls the iPhone and its NFC chip, so it decides who can offer tap-to-pay on iPhone. Being the default on every iPhone gives it a habit no bank app can match. Regulators in the EU (2024) and the UK (2026 proposal) are weakening this moat by forcing NFC access.

competitors.name: Google Wallet

competitors.name: Bank tap-to-pay apps in the EU

competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Apple Pay is the default and simpler; bank apps avoid Apple's fees.

competitors.name: PayPal
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Apple Pay is faster on iPhone; PayPal works on any device and offers buyer protection.

competitors.name: Curve Pay
competitors.positioning: Wallet that sits on top of all your cards.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Curve depends on Apple's NFC access, now owned by Lloyds.

competitors.name: UPI (India, for comparison)
competitors.positioning: India's free, instant bank-to-bank payment system, used by QR code.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: UPI has zero fees and runs on any phone; cards are less common in India, which is one reason Apple Pay has not launched there.

northStar.why: It shows Apple Pay is part of people's daily lives, which is what keeps them on iPhone. This is a better north star metric than fee revenue, which is small and depends on bank deals.

pmLessons: Owning the platform gives huge power, but regulators may limit it if rivals are blocked.
A feature can be worth more for loyalty than for direct revenue; Apple Pay keeps people on iPhone.
Make the default the easiest choice, and most users will never change it.
Payments habits are local: what works in London may not work in India, where UPI rules.

interviewQuestions.question: How should Apple respond to the UK CMA's proposal to open NFC?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh security, fee revenue, iPhone loyalty and regulatory goodwill. Look at what happened in the EU after 2024. Suggest a clear plan.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Apple Pay launch in India? How?
interviewQuestions.hint: Look at iPhone share, UPI's dominance, RBI rules on data and payments, and bank partners. A UPI-first launch may make more sense than cards.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you measure Apple Pay's success if fee revenue is small?
interviewQuestions.hint: Active payers, payments per user, retention of iPhone users who use Apple Pay versus those who do not.

interviewQuestions.question: Why do you think Apple shut down Apple Pay Later?
interviewQuestions.hint: Credit risk, regulation, cost of being a lender, and a move to partner with existing lenders like Klarna and Affirm instead.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature to increase online Apple Pay use.
interviewQuestions.hint: Find why merchants do not add it and why users skip it. Ideas: easier merchant setup, loyalty cards at checkout. Metric: online payments per user.
